system_message:
You are generating a synthetic but clinically grounded
conversation for exactly one hospital admission.

Rules:
1. Use only facts supported by the provided admission context.
2. The discharge notes are the backbone of the hospital-course
   narrative. Use them first.
3. The ordered problem list should shape the main clinical focus.
4. Radiology, procedures, microbiology, and the previous-admission
   summary are supporting context, not a checklist.
5. Not every packet item needs to appear in the conversation.
6. Speakers must be exactly: Doctor and Patient.
7. Every conversation line must contain:
   - turn number
   - exact timestamp
   - speaker
   - text
8. Timestamps must be monotonically increasing and stay within the
   admission start and admission end times.
9. Keep the conversation medically plausible and understandable to
   a patient.
10. Use short natural exchanges, patient questions, clarifications,
    explanations, reassurance, and follow-up discussion.
11. Do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, test findings,
    or outcomes.
12. Do not mention the dataset, packet, note types, or that the
    conversation is synthetic.
13. Generate the conversation first, then write the summary strictly from the generated conversation_lines.
14. Every claim in summary.summary_paragraph and every item in summary.problems must be explicitly supported by the conversation_lines.
15. Return output that exactly matches the required JSON schema.
task_message:
Generate one rich patient-doctor conversation for this admission and one admission summary.

Generation guidance:
- Approximate stay length: 7 day(s).
- Recommended turn range: 50-70 turns.
- Exact admission window: 2152-01-17 16:18:00 to 2152-01-23 16:30:00.
- Focus first on the discharge-note storyline and the core admission problems.
- Use radiology, procedures, and microbiology only as supporting detail when they help the story.
- Do not try to mention every packet item.
- Let the conversation unfold across admission, mid-course updates, and discharge planning.
- Prefer many short natural exchanges over a few long summary turns.
- The patient should ask questions, express concerns, seek clarification, and respond to updates throughout the stay.
- The doctor should explain results, treatment changes, progress, and follow-up in multiple conversational beats over time.
- You may paraphrase and add natural conversational glue, but do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, findings, or outcomes.
- Generate the conversation first, then derive the final summary only from the conversation_lines you wrote.
- The final summary must contain admission start time, admission end time, one paragraph summary, and a list of problems.
- Final self-check before returning JSON: turn_number contiguous from 1; conversation_lines.time nondecreasing and inside the exact admission window; summary.admission_start and summary.admission_end copied exactly from the packet; no conversation line has empty text.

previous_admission_summary_used.summary_paragraph: The patient was admitted for her third cycle of high-dose methotrexate for diffuse large B-cell lymphoma with CNS involvement. She tolerated the chemotherapy well and cleared the drug within 48 hours. During the admission, she developed abdominal pain and increased ostomy output, prompting imaging and stool studies. A CT scan showed bowel wall edema and pneumatosis, and a stool test confirmed Clostridium difficile infection, for which she was treated with oral vancomycin. Her symptoms resolved by discharge. Her diabetes was managed with insulin due to elevated blood sugars in the hospital, though she was not discharged on insulin due to hypoglycemia risk. She received IVIG for CVID and completed a dose of Neupogen to support white blood cell recovery. She was discharged home with follow-up arranged and instructions to complete her vancomycin course.
problems: Intestinal infection due to Clostridium difficile
Other malignant lymphomas, unspecified site, extranodal and solid organ sites
Diabetes mellitus without mention of complication, type II or unspecified type, not stated as uncontrolled

Brief Hospital Course:
___ year old female with a history of type 2 diabetes, common 
variable immunodeficiency on chronic IVIG since ___, chronic 
back pain, and primary colonic diffuse large B-cell lymphoma s/p 
small bowel resection with CNS involvement with recent C. diff 
infection on previous hospitalization, now presenting for 
high-dose MTX #4 for CNS lymphoma.
.
#. Primary colonic DLBCL: Admitted for MTX infusion cycle #4.  
Previously complicated by mucositis (cycle #1), so lower dose 
was given once again.  A pre-infusion CXR ruled out pleural 
effusions and maintenance fluids with NaHCO3 was given to keep 
urine pH >7, with frequent checks.  Methotrexate levels were 
monitored at 24, 48, and 72 hours post-infusion and decreased 
accordingly s/p infusion.  Leucovorin rescuse was given starting 
24 hours s/p MTX infusion.  The patient developed mild mucositis 
that was controlled with caphasol and Gelclair.  We felt there 
was an element of candidiasis to her oral lesions, so she was 
started on Fluconazole and will continue on this 
prophylactically as an outpatient.
.
#. C. diff and electrolyte abnormalities: She was previous 
discharged with PO Vancomycin for known C. diff positivity.  Her 
diarrhea had slowed down as an outpatient and she continued to 
take the Vancomycin as prescribed.  However, flatus and 
increased stool output complicated her hospital visit, but she 
found that taking Bean-o (as she had at home) was more effective 
than simethicone.  Her stools were ""foamy"" so stool studies were 
sent and returned negative.  She was also given a 3-day course 
of rifaximin to try control bacterial overgrowth secondary to 
hyperglycemia and short-gut.  She was continued on Vanc PO 125mg 
PO q6h for the duration of her stay and will continue on this at 
the discretion of her outpatient providers, instead of 14-day 
course.  Due to high ostomy output, K+ and Mg+ were repleted 
aggressively and she was sent home with supplementation.  IVF 
was continued as above to prevent dehydration
.
#. t2DM and hyperglycemia: At home, her diabetes is usually 
well-controlled with only metformin and diet.  While an 
inpatient, we held her metformin and started an ISS while in 
house.  She required 20 units of Lantus and an aggressive ISS in 
order to control her sugars, since we felt that it was more 
important for her to eat what she wanted due to her cachexia, 
than to restrict her to a diabetic diet.  Her FSBGs ran in the 
high 200s to 300s consistently, but she assured us that she 
would eat healthier and take her blood sugars often upon 
discharge.
.
#. Chronic back pain: Patient has back and leg pain all of the 
time and is managed with a regimen of medications that seems to 
keep her pain under control.  She was continued on methadone, 
oxycodone, and cyclobenzaprine.
.
#. Follow-up:  Her pentamidine PCP prophylaxis will be due as an 
outpatient on ___ (given last on ___.  She will also likely 
need IVIG as outpatient in the near future for her 
immunodeficiency.  She was provided only with a week's worth of 
narcotics and benzos and an e-mail was sent to her PCP, the 
purveyor of her narcotics contract.

Brief Hospital Course:
___ year old female with a history of type 2 diabetes, common 
variable immunodeficiency on chronic IVIG since ___, chronic 
back pain, and primary colonic diffuse large B-cell lymphoma s/p 
small bowel resection with CNS involvement with recent C. diff 
infection on previous hospitalization, now presenting for 
high-dose MTX #4 for CNS lymphoma.
.
#. Primary colonic DLBCL: Admitted for MTX infusion cycle #4.  
Previously complicated by mucositis (cycle #1), so lower dose 
was given once again.  A pre-infusion CXR ruled out pleural 
effusions and maintenance fluids with NaHCO3 was given to keep 
urine pH >7, with frequent checks.  Methotrexate levels were 
monitored at 24, 48, and 72 hours post-infusion and decreased 
accordingly s/p infusion.  Leucovorin rescuse was given starting 
24 hours s/p MTX infusion.  The patient developed mild mucositis 
that was controlled with caphasol and Gelclair.  We felt there 
was an element of candidiasis to her oral lesions, so she was 
started on Fluconazole and will continue on this 
prophylactically as an outpatient.
.
#. C. diff and electrolyte abnormalities: She was previous 
discharged with PO Vancomycin for known C. diff positivity.  Her 
diarrhea had slowed down as an outpatient and she continued to 
take the Vancomycin as prescribed.  However, flatus and 
increased stool output complicated her hospital visit, but she 
found that taking Bean-o (as she had at home) was more effective 
than simethicone.  Her stools were ""foamy"" so stool studies were 
sent and returned negative.  She was also given a 3-day course 
of rifaximin to try control bacterial overgrowth secondary to 
hyperglycemia and short-gut.  She was continued on Vanc PO 125mg 
PO q6h for the duration of her stay and will continue on this at 
the discretion of her outpatient providers, instead of 14-day 
course.  Due to high ostomy output, K+ and Mg+ were repleted 
aggressively and she was sent home with supplementation.  IVF 
was continued as above to prevent dehydration
.
#. t2DM and hyperglycemia: At home, her diabetes is usually 
well-controlled with only metformin and diet.  While an 
inpatient, we held her metformin and started an ISS while in 
house.  She required 20 units of Lantus and an aggressive ISS in 
order to control her sugars, since we felt that it was more 
important for her to eat what she wanted due to her cachexia, 
than to restrict her to a diabetic diet.  Her FSBGs ran in the 
high 200s to 300s consistently, but she assured us that she 
would eat healthier and take her blood sugars often upon 
discharge.
.
#. Chronic back pain: Patient has back and leg pain all of the 
time and is managed with a regimen of medications that seems to 
keep her pain under control.  She was continued on methadone, 
oxycodone, and cyclobenzaprine.
.
#. Follow-up:  Her pentamidine PCP prophylaxis will be due as an 
outpatient on ___ (given last on ___.  She will also likely 
need IVIG as outpatient in the near future for her 
immunodeficiency.  She was provided only with a week's worth of 
narcotics and benzos and an e-mail was sent to her PCP, the 
purveyor of her narcotics contract.

methotrexate blood levels decreased appropriately and you were 
discharged with close follow-up with your primary oncology team.

1) START fluconazole for protection against fungal infections 
when your cell counts are low

your cell counts are low

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, Ms. ___. I'm Dr. ___ from the oncology team. We're admitting you today for your fourth cycle of high-dose methotrexate for your lymphoma. How have you been feeling since your last discharge?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Hi, Doctor. I’ve been more tired than usual and passing a lot of gas. My ostomy output has slowed down a bit, but it’s still more than normal. No fevers or nausea, though.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That makes sense. We know you were on vancomycin for C. diff from your last admission. Are you still taking it?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, I’ve been taking it every six hours like they told me. It helped, but I still have some gas and foamy stools.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Okay, we’ll keep you on the vancomycin during this stay. We’ll also check a stool sample to make sure the C. diff is fully cleared.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Should I be worried if it’s still positive?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Not necessarily. Sometimes the test can stay positive even after the infection is gone. We’ll focus on your symptoms and whether your output improves.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s a relief. My back pain is also acting up—same as always. I’ve been using my usual meds.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll continue your methadone, oxycodone, and cyclobenzaprine. Pain control is important, especially during chemo.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you. I’m also a bit nervous about the methotrexate—last time I had bad mouth sores.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I understand. That’s why we’re using a lower dose again—3500 mg/m² instead of 8000. We’ll also start leucovorin 24 hours after the infusion to help protect your cells.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the fluids with baking soda? I remember that from last time.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. We’ll give you IV fluids with sodium bicarbonate to keep your urine alkaline. That helps your kidneys clear the methotrexate safely.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it. What about my blood sugar? It’s been high at home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll monitor it closely. We’ve held your metformin for now and will use insulin to keep your sugars in check. You need good nutrition, so we don’t want to restrict your diet.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That sounds good. I’ve been trying to eat more, but it’s hard with the fatigue.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll support you with IV fluids and nutrition as needed. Let’s get you settled, and I’ll come back after the chest X-ray.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your chest X-ray looks clear—no fluid or infection. That’s great. We’re cleared to start the methotrexate infusion tomorrow morning.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good to hear. Any other tests today?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We drew blood for labs, including your kidney and liver function. Your potassium is a bit low, so we’ll start replacing it with IV fluids.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve been losing a lot through the ostomy. Should I take supplements?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we’ll start oral potassium and magnesium. You’ll go home with those too, to help keep your levels stable.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. We’re about to start your methotrexate infusion. Any new symptoms?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No, just the usual back pain. I’m ready when you are.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll begin now. The infusion will take a few hours. We’ll monitor your urine pH and keep you well-hydrated.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Infusion is complete. You did well. We’ll start checking your methotrexate levels tomorrow and the day after.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thanks. My mouth already feels a little dry.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll start using Caphasol and Gelclair to keep your mouth moist and prevent sores. We also noticed some white patches—could be early thrush.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is that serious?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Not serious, but we want to treat it. We’re starting fluconazole to clear it up and prevent it from coming back during your low counts.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your stool test came back negative for C. diff toxin. That’s good news—means the infection is likely resolving.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So I can stop the vancomycin?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll keep you on it for now. Your output is still high, and with your short gut, we want to be cautious. We’re also starting a short course of rifaximin to help with bacterial overgrowth.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your first methotrexate level is 0.54, which is expected. It’s coming down appropriately.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the leucovorin?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Started last night, and we’ll continue it until your levels are undetectable. It helps protect your healthy cells.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: My mouth feels sore. The patches are spreading a bit.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s mild mucositis, common with methotrexate. Keep using the Caphasol and Gelclair. The fluconazole will help with the fungal component.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your second methotrexate level is 0.02—great. It’s clearing well. Your kidney function is stable.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my blood sugar?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Still running high—mostly in the 200s and 300s. We’re keeping you on insulin. We’ll transition back to metformin at home, but we need to control it now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll try to eat better when I’m home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We know it’s tough. Your nutrition is more important right now than perfect sugar control. We’ll support you.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your last methotrexate level is <0.02—undetectable. That means you’ve cleared the drug safely. Great job.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s a relief. My mouth is feeling better too.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The fluconazole and mouth care are working. We’ll send it home with you as a preventive measure.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re planning to discharge you tomorrow. Your labs are stable, and you’re doing well overall.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What about the vancomycin and supplements?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll continue vancomycin at home as directed by your outpatient team. We’re sending potassium and magnesium supplements with refills.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the fluconazole?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, one tablet daily to prevent fungal infections when your counts are low. We’re also adding acyclovir for viral protection.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. Any follow-up tests?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll need IVIG for your immune deficiency and pentamidine for PCP prophylaxis. Your oncology team will coordinate that.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. We’ve reviewed everything, and you’re cleared to go home today.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Great. Any final instructions?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Continue all new medications as prescribed. Monitor your blood sugar, stay hydrated, and call if you develop fever, worsening mouth sores, or abdominal pain.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Thank you for taking care of me.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. We’ll see you in follow-up soon. Take care.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Just confirming—I take the potassium once a day and magnesium twice a day?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, exactly. And the fluconazole and acyclovir daily. Your pharmacy will have all the details.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it. I feel ready to go home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll have your discharge papers and prescriptions ready shortly. Rest well.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: The nurse said my ostomy bag needs changing every few days. Is that right?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, and keep an eye on the skin around it. If it gets red or sore, use the barrier cream we sent home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will do. Thanks again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re all set. Take it easy and follow up with your team.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Have a good day.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You too. See you soon.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: One last thing—when should I restart my regular pain meds routine?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re already on them—methadone, oxycodone, and cyclobenzaprine. Just follow the discharge instructions and call if pain worsens.

summary.summary_paragraph: The patient was admitted for her fourth cycle of high-dose methotrexate for primary colonic diffuse large B-cell lymphoma with CNS involvement. She had a history of C. difficile infection from a prior admission and was continuing oral vancomycin. During this stay, her stool tested negative for C. difficile toxin, but she had ongoing high ostomy output, prompting electrolyte repletion and a short course of rifaximin for possible bacterial overgrowth. Methotrexate was administered at a reduced dose of 3500 mg/m², with leucovorin rescue started 24 hours post-infusion. Methotrexate levels declined appropriately, and she developed mild mucositis with oral candidiasis, treated with fluconazole and oral care products. Her diabetes was managed with insulin due to persistent hyperglycemia, though she was transitioned back to metformin at discharge. She was discharged home with continued vancomycin, new prescriptions for fluconazole and acyclovir for prophylaxis, and supplements for potassium and magnesium.
